body.title: Privacy
body.summary: What this website collects, which is almost nothing, and what happens to it.
body.body:
The association runs this website for the people who live in Discovery. It is
built to collect as little as possible about you, and most of the time it
collects nothing at all.

## Reading the website

Nothing is collected when you read these pages. There is no analytics, no
tracking, no advertising, and no cookie set by this site. Every font, image and
style sheet is served from the association's own site, so reading a page here
does not tell any other company that you were here.

## What the host records

The site is hosted by Cloudflare, which keeps a short-lived record of requests
to it — the address the request came from, the page asked for, and the time.
That is ordinary server logging, used to keep the site up and to investigate
abuse. The board does not use it to identify residents and does not combine it
with anything else.

## The email list

If you sign up for board news, the association keeps your email address and
uses it to send you agendas and notices, about once a month. It is not shared,
sold, or used for anything else. Every message has an unsubscribe link, and you
can also ask the office to remove you.

## Signing in

The board's own administration app is separate, and only invited board members
and volunteers can sign in to it. It uses a Google account, so the association
never handles or stores a password. It stores the person's name and email
address, the roles they hold, and a session that expires. Nobody can create an
account for themselves.

## Documents on the site

Agendas, forms, plans and rules published here are records the board has chosen
to make public. Approved minutes are not published here; they are filed in the
resident portal instead.

## Who else sees any of this

Nobody. The association does not sell or share resident information, and does
not use advertising or analytics services.

## Asking about your information

Write to the office at the address on the contact page and ask. If you are on
the email list and want off it, say so and it will be done.

body.title: Terms of use
body.summary: The plain terms for using this website, and what governs when they disagree.
body.body:
This website is published by Discovery Homeowners Association, Inc. for the
people who live in Discovery. These are the plain terms for using it.

## What the site is for

It is where the association publishes what residents need to know: when the
board meets, what the rules are, how to pay dues, who to call, and what is being
worked on.

## What it is not

It is a convenience, not the record. Where this website and the association's
recorded governing documents disagree, **the recorded documents govern**, and so
do the official minutes of the board. Nothing here is legal advice. If a
decision matters to you — a fee, a deadline, an architectural approval — check
the governing documents or ask the office.

## Keeping it accurate

The board keeps these pages current and corrects mistakes when it learns of
them. Dates, fees and schedules do change. If you find something wrong, please
report it; the contact page says how.

## Using the site fairly

Read it, print it, and share it freely with your neighbors. Do not try to break
into it, overload it, or use its forms to send anything other than what they
ask for.

## The board's administration app

The administration app is for invited board members and volunteers, and access
is granted by the board. Signing in to it, or trying to, without that invitation
is not permitted.

## Links to other places

Some pages link to the county, to utilities, and to the resident portal where
dues are paid and minutes are filed. Those are run by other organizations, under
their own terms and their own privacy practices.

## Changes

These terms change when the site does. The current version is always the one on
this page.

body.title: About Discovery
body.summary: How the neighborhood came to be, and the people who keep it running.
body.body:
Discovery is a neighborhood of single-family homes and townhouses in
Walkersville, Maryland — about 160 acres, laid out in 1972 as Frederick County's
first planned unit development.

The association owns and looks after the things no single household does: the
pool, the Recreation Center, the RV lot, and roughly twenty parks and open
spaces.

body.title: Amenities
body.summary: The pool, the Recreation Center, the RV lot, and twenty parks — all paid for by your assessment.
body.body:
These are the things the association owns on everyone's behalf. Your assessment
maintains them, and residents in good standing can use them.

body.title: Exterior Changes (ACC)
body.summary: Anything you change on the outside of your home needs approval first. Here is what that covers and how to ask.
body.body:
If you are changing anything on the outside of your home, send the Architectural
Control Committee an application **before** the work starts.

That is the whole rule, and it is worth taking seriously in the order given.
Approval after the fact is a much harder conversation than approval beforehand,
and the committee would far rather review a drawing than send a non-compliance
letter.

## Why this exists

The ACC is six neighbors, not an office. What they are protecting is the thing
that made anyone buy here: a neighborhood that looks cared for and holds its
value. A fence that sits three feet into a common area, or a roof color nobody
else has, costs somebody money eventually — sometimes the person who installed
it, when they try to sell.

Most applications are approved. The ones that are not usually turn out to be
misunderstandings about where a property line runs.

## How to apply

Ask the office for the current **Application for Exterior Change**, or email the
committee directly at {{email:acc}}. Send it in with a sketch or a
photograph and the materials you plan to use. If you are not sure whether your
project needs approval, ask — it takes one email and saves a lot of bother.

<aside class="callout callout--note">

If you need help filling out the application, call the office at

{{phone:office}} and the manager will put you in touch with someone who
can walk you through it.

</aside>

<section lang="es">

Si está pensando en realizar algún trabajo en el exterior de su casa — cercas,
patios, terrazas, ventanas, puertas delanteras y mosquiteras, puertas
corredizas, paneles solares, revestimientos, techos, canaletas y puertas de
garaje — por favor complete una solicitud **antes** de comenzar el trabajo. No
queremos enviar cartas de incumplimiento.

Si necesita ayuda llenando la solicitud, por favor contacte a la oficina y la
gerente lo pondrá en contacto con una persona que le ayude. Gracias.

</section>

## If you get a letter

A non-compliance letter is not a fine and it is not the end of the conversation.
It comes with a response form — fill it in and send it back. Most cases close
there.

## Parking, trailers, and boats

This is the other thing the committee spends its time on, and it is governed by
the association's recorded documents rather than by committee preference. The
relevant passages are quoted below so you can read the actual language rather
than a summary of it.

The board meets on the third Tuesday of every month at the Recreation Center,

commitment.

body.title: History
body.summary: Discovery was Frederick County's first planned unit development, built on 160 acres of farmland starting in 1972.
body.body:
In 1972, four miles outside Frederick City, a 160-acre tract of farmland became
Frederick County's first planned unit development.

That phrase — _planned unit development_ — was doing real work at the time. The
conventional approach was to divide land into lots and let the amenities work
themselves out. Discovery was drawn the other way round: housing, parks, and
shared facilities laid out together from the start, as one thing.

## What was drawn

The master plan called for 255 single-family houses and 400 townhouses, a
6.5-acre shopping center, a swimming pool, tennis courts, a day care center, and
recreational facilities scattered through the neighborhood rather than gathered
at one edge of it.

Not all of it survived contact with the next fifty years. The shopping center
and the day care are no longer part of the association. The pool, the Recreation
Center, and about twenty parks and open spaces are — and they are still the
reason the association exists.

## The streets

Whoever named the streets committed to the theme completely, and the result is
one of the more cheerful street grids in the county: Revelation Avenue, Inquiry
Court, Dream Place, Discovery Place, Discovery Boulevard, Seekers Walk, Daring
Court, Inspiration Court. Later sections kept it up — Eureka Lane, Foresight
Lane, Imagination Court, Curiosity Court, Triumphant Court, Successful Way.

The bare ground in the photograph above is now front yards.

## Still run by the people who live here

Fifty years on, Discovery is not managed by a company that also manages forty
other neighborhoods. It is run by a board of directors who live on these
streets, meet monthly in the Recreation Center, and are elected by their
neighbors.

That is worth knowing when something goes wrong: the person you end up talking
to almost certainly drives past the problem too.

body.title: Home
body.summary: Discovery Homeowners Association in Walkersville, Maryland — assessments, the pool, the Recreation Center, architectural approvals, and how to reach the office.
body.body:
## Welcome to Discovery

Discovery is a neighborhood of single-family homes and townhouses in
Walkersville, Maryland. When ground was broken in 1972 it was the first planned
unit development in Frederick County — a deliberate mix of housing, parks, and
shared amenities on about 160 acres of former farmland.

The association exists to look after the things no single household owns: the
pool, the Recreation Center, the RV lot, and roughly twenty parks and open
spaces. It is run by a volunteer board of directors elected by the people who
live here, and it is funded by the annual assessment.

## New to the neighborhood?

Three things are worth knowing in your first week.

**Get approval before you change the outside of your home.** Fences, decks,
sheds, windows, doors, siding, roofing, solar panels — anything visible from
outside needs an Architectural Control Committee application first. It is a
short form, and it protects your investment as much as your neighbor's.
[Start here](/rules/architectural-control/).

**Set up your account in the resident portal.** You can pay your assessment,
pull up association documents, and send questions to the office without a stamp.

**Come to a board meeting.** They are held monthly and every homeowner and
renter is welcome — you do not need a reason or an invitation to attend.

body.title: Meetings
body.summary: The board meets monthly and every homeowner and renter is welcome. No invitation needed.
body.body:
The board of directors meets on the third Tuesday of every month at the
Recreation Center.

**Any homeowner or renter can attend.** You do not need to be on an agenda, ask
permission, or have a complaint. People come to listen, and that is a perfectly
good reason to be there.

## What gets discussed

The recurring business is money and maintenance: the budget, contracts for
landscaping and trash, the pool season, park repairs, and whatever project is
currently in flight. Architectural Control matters are handled by that committee
and come to the board when they need a decision.

## Bringing something up

If you have a question or a proposal, two things make it go better. Email the
office beforehand so it can go on the agenda — {{email:general}} — and
bring the specifics: the address, the date, the photo. Boards can act on
specifics and can only nod sympathetically at generalities.

body.title: Parks & Playgrounds
body.summary: Twenty parks and open spaces, inspected once a year and maintained by the association.
body.body:
Twenty parks and open spaces are scattered through the neighborhood — the tot
lots between the townhouse courts, the open greens, and the paths connecting
them. They are association property, which means they are paid for out of your
assessment and maintained on your behalf.

## Reporting something broken

Do not wait for the annual inspection. If a swing is hanging by one chain or a
slide has a crack in it, tell the office and it gets logged and scheduled.

body.title: Community Pool
body.summary: Season dates, hours, membership fees, and the rules that keep it pleasant.
body.body:
The pool is the reason a lot of people picked this neighborhood, and it is the
association's busiest amenity by a wide margin.

The full rules are posted at the gate and included with the online application.
The four below are the ones the lifeguards spend their summer repeating.

body.title: Projects

body.body:
The association is a volunteer board with a finite budget, so work is sequenced
rather than done all at once. This is what is actually in progress.

Feedback genuinely does change what gets prioritized. Come to a
[monthly meeting](/meetings/) or email {{email:general}}.

body.summary: Rent the Rec Center for a party, a meeting, or a family gathering. Capacity 49.
body.body:
The Recreation Center at 8740 Stauffer Road is available to rent for birthdays,
showers, meetings, and family gatherings.

Book it through the office at least a week ahead. You will get the door code
when the rental fee and deposit are paid.

The deposit comes back after someone from the association walks through and
finds the place in good order. It is forfeited if the occupancy limit was
exceeded — that one is a fire code violation and the association has no
discretion about it.

Renters who do not own their home need written permission from their landlord;
there is a separate form for that, signed at the same time as the contract.

body.body:
Different problems go to different places, and calling the wrong one costs you a
day. This is the whole list, most urgent first.

<aside class="callout callout--warning">

For anything immediate, urgent, or life-threatening, call **911**. Do not call
the office first.

</aside>

body.title: Rules & Requests
body.summary: Exterior changes, trash and recycling, and who to call when something is wrong.
body.body:
Most of what the association asks of residents comes down to three things: get
approval before you change the outside of your home, put the bins out at the
right time, and tell someone when something is broken.

body.title: RV Lot
body.summary: Storage for boats, trailers, and recreational vehicles. There is a monthly fee, and registration is enforced.
body.body:
The association keeps a lot where residents can store boats, trailers, and
recreational vehicles instead of leaving them on the street or in a driveway.

## There is now a fee

The RV lot used to be free. It is not any more — the association began charging
for it on 1 October 2025, and the fee is what will eventually pay for repairing
the fence and marking out the spaces.

## Registration is not optional

If you have anything in the RV lot, it has to be registered with the office.

<aside class="callout callout--warning">

Anything in the lot that is not registered with the office is towed by Dorsey's
Towing, at the owner's expense. There is no warning notice first.

</aside>

Registration is straightforward — the form, a copy of the vehicle's
registration, and a photo. Ask the office for the current application, or call

{{phone:office}}.

<section lang="es">

**Solicitud de lote para vehículos recreativos**

Si tiene un barco, un remolque o cualquier otro vehículo recreativo en el lote,
debe enviar el formulario junto con el certificado de registro y una foto. Por
favor, envíenos esta información antes de la fecha límite.

Desde el 1 de octubre de 2025 el lote ya no es gratuito: la tarifa es de **$50
por mes** o **$150 por trimestre**, pagadera junto con su cuota trimestral.

Todos los vehículos en el lote que no estén registrados en la oficina serán
remolcados por Dorsey's Towing a cargo del propietario.

</section>

body.title: Trash & Recycling
body.summary: Collection days, what belongs in yard waste, and why recycling keeps your assessment down.
body.body:
Trash goes out Tuesday and Friday mornings. Recycling alternates depending on
which side of Stauffer Road you live on, and yard waste runs twice a month from
April to December.

The full schedule is below. If you are new, the county's lookup tool will tell
you your exact recycling week by address.

## Containers

Animals are the reason this rule exists. A bag left at the curb overnight is an
invitation, and whoever finds the mess in the morning is usually not the person
who put the bag out.

body.title: Welcome Committee
body.summary: New neighbors get a knock on the door and a friendly face. Volunteers welcome.
body.body:
Moving in is disorienting. You do not know which day the trash goes out, where
the pool passes come from, or who to ask about the fence you were planning to
put up.

The Welcome Committee exists to shorten that. Someone stops by, says hello,
answers the obvious questions, and points you at the less obvious ones.

## Help out

This is one of the easiest ways to get involved in the neighborhood. It costs an
hour here and there, it does not require a skill you have to already have, and
new neighbors remember it.

Email {{email:general}} and they will connect you with
the right person.

## Just moved in?

Start with three things:

1. **[Get approval before changing anything outside your home](/rules/architectural-control/)** — fences, sheds, doors, windows, roofing.
2. **Set up your account in the resident portal** so you can pay your assessment and pull up documents online.
3. **[Come to a board meeting](/meetings/)** — every homeowner and renter is welcome, no invitation needed.
